description: Jason leaves Medea for a princess. She kills their children. Euripides creates a heroine who is terrifying, brilliant and foreign: passion turns into reasoning.

hero.hook: A woman betrayed. An ice-cold calculation. Greek theater never got over the shock.

blocks.text: In **431 BC**, in Athens, **Euripides**, one of the three great writers of Greek tragedy, presents **Medea**. **Jason**, the Greek hero who led the [[Argonauts]] on their legendary voyage aboard the ship Argo, has sworn to stay faithful to **Medea**, the sorceress who helped him seize the **Golden Fleece**. At **Corinth**, he leaves her to marry the king's daughter.

Medea does not simply weep. She plans an absolute revenge. Euripides puts at the center a woman who speaks, calculates and chooses the irreparable. The play shocked its first audience. It is still one of the most feared tragedies in the repertoire.

Beside [[Aeschylus]], the first of the three great tragedians and author of the Oresteia, and [[Sophocles]], author of Oedipus the King, Euripides explores the inner life. His characters doubt, contradict themselves and justify the unjustifiable. Athenian audiences sometimes found him too cynical. Later readers saw in him a genius of dramatic psychology.

blocks.caption: Medea by Delacroix: a mother's tenderness and the decision to kill

blocks.text: Medea is not a silent fury. She **argues**. That is what frightens. Euripides gives her brilliant speeches on the injustice done to women, on betrayal, on shame. The monster speaks with a disturbing clarity.

sections.title: Euripides, the most “modern” of the three

blocks.text: To Greek eyes Medea is a [[Barbarian]]. The word meant anyone who did not speak Greek. Here it means a woman from **Colchis**, a distant land on the Black Sea. She betrayed her own people for Jason. When he casts her off, she loses her status, her protection and her future. [[The figure of the stranger in Greek tragedy]] turns explosive here: the outsider knows the rules better than the people who make them.
Jason owes her everything: without Medea's spells, no Golden Fleece. Euripides insists on it. The “civilized” man behaves like an ingrate, while the foreign woman pays for her broken loyalty.

blocks.caption: Jason and the Golden Fleece: the hero succeeds thanks to Medea

sections.title: The foreign woman whose pact is broken

blocks.text: Medea hesitates. She loves her sons. Then she decides: killing them strikes Jason at the heart, where Greek family honor hurts most. [[Thumos]], the angry part of the soul, the seat of rage and courage, wins out. But it wins inside a clear-eyed speech. This is no silent fit of madness. It is an ice-cold calculation, chosen after a wrenching monologue.

At the end comes a [[Deus ex machina]]: Medea escapes on a winged chariot sent by her grandfather the **Sun**, the god **Helios**. The device brings in a divine force to untie the action. There is no immediate punishment. The unease stays in the theater. The audience goes out troubled, with no simple moral answer.

sections.title: Killing her children: reason against passion?

blocks.text: From **Seneca**, the Latin tragedian, to **Pasolini**, the Italian filmmaker, from **Corneille**, the French playwright of the 17th century, to the stages of today, Medea keeps coming back. Readers find revenge in her, and feminism, colonization, the rage of abandonment. Euripides does not excuse infanticide. He forces us to hear the voice of the woman who commits it.

Euripides also lets us feel the political cost of the act: Medea strikes Jason, but she also strikes the future of the city by destroying his line. The **chorus**, a group of Corinthian women who comment on the action, hovers between pity and horror. That ambivalence is the strength of the play: we understand without absolving, we shudder without being able to look away.
**Medea** by Euripides shows how a private injustice can become an absolute catastrophe. The betrayed foreigner reasons her way to revenge, and Greek theater discovers a heroine nobody can file away.

sections.title: A heroine who keeps disturbing us
